title: Agency
outcomes: Define agent and principal (Section 182), state who may appoint and who may be an agent, and explain the modes of creating an agency, including ratification and estoppel.
Explain the extent of an agent's authority in normal situations and emergencies, and distinguish a sub-agent from a substituted agent.
State the duties and rights of an agent and compute amounts an agent may retain or must account for.
Explain the principal's liability to third parties, the cases where an agent is personally liable, and the modes and effects of termination of agency, including irrevocable agency.

meta.exam_tip: Frequent problems: minor as agent (Section 184), ratification (Sections 196–200), emergency authority (Section 189), agent dealing on own account (Sections 215–216), sub-agent liability (Sections 192–193), personal liability of agent (Section 230) and irrevocable agency (Section 202).

concepts.title: Agent and principal (Sections 182–185)
body: Section 182: an agent is someone engaged to act for another, or to stand in for him in dealings with outsiders; the person for whom the act is done, or who is represented, is the principal. The Act does not define "agency" itself. The test is whether the person can bind the principal and create privity of contract between the principal and third parties. The idea: he who acts through another acts himself.
Section 183: anyone who is a major under the law applicable to him and of sound mind may employ an agent — so minors and persons of unsound mind are unable to have agents of their own.

Section 184: as between the principal and third persons, anyone may become an agent — even a minor or a person of unsound mind — and the principal is bound by his acts. But such an agent is not responsible to the principal for his conduct, so the principal has no remedy against him.
Section 185: no consideration is needed to create an agency.
concepts.analogy: An agent is the principal's extended arm: what the arm signs, the body is bound by.
concepts.work: Companies act only through agents — directors, managers, sales staff. Before relying on a document, a CA checks that the signatory had authority to bind the company.

concepts.title: Creation of agency
body: Express agency: authority given by spoken or written words, e.g. a power of attorney (Sections 186–187).

Implied agency: authority inferred from the circumstances, conduct or the ordinary course of dealing (Section 187). Two important forms: (a) agency by estoppel (Section 237) — if the principal's words or conduct lead a third person to believe that someone is his agent and the third person acts on that belief, the principal cannot later deny the agency; (b) agency of necessity — in an emergency, a person already in charge of another's goods may act to save them (for example, a caretaker spends money to put out a fire on the owner's farm).
Agency by operation of law: the law itself treats one person as another's agent — for instance, every partner is the agent of the firm for the business of the firm.
Agency by ratification (Sections 196–200): a person may adopt an act done on his behalf without authority; once ratified, it is as if authorised from the start.
concepts.analogy: Agency can be born from a signed letter, from silence that misleads, from a crisis, or from a later "yes, I approve".
concepts.work: Where an employee has habitually placed orders with a supplier and the company has always paid, the company may be bound by estoppel even after it secretly withdrew the employee's authority — a common issue CAs see in disputed payables.

concepts.title: Ratification (Sections 196–200)
body: If someone acts for another without authority, the other may ratify or disown the act (Section 196). Ratification may be express or implied from conduct — for example, accepting interest on money lent without authority (Section 197).

Conditions: (1) the act must have been done on behalf of the principal, not for the actor himself; (2) the principal must have existed and been competent both when the act was done and when he ratifies; (3) the principal must have full knowledge of the material facts (Section 198); (4) the whole transaction must be ratified, not just the favourable part (Section 199); (5) ratification cannot subject a third person to damages or end his rights or interests (Section 200); (6) it must be made within a reasonable time and communicated; and (7) the act must be one the principal could lawfully have done — a void or illegal act (e.g. forgery) cannot be ratified.
Effect: ratification relates back to the date of the act — the contract binds as if made with authority.
concepts.analogy: Ratification is signing a photograph after it is taken: it becomes your picture from the moment the shutter clicked — but you cannot sign only half the photo.
concepts.work: Board meetings often "ratify" purchases made by an executive beyond his limit. A CA checks that the board was told all material facts; otherwise the ratification may not bind.

concepts.title: Extent of authority (Sections 188, 189)
body: Section 188: authority to do an act carries with it authority for every lawful step needed to get it done; authority to run a business covers every lawful step needed for it or customarily taken in running such a business.

Section 189: in an emergency, an agent may do all acts to protect his principal from loss that a person of ordinary prudence would do in his own case in similar circumstances. Conditions: the agent could not communicate with the principal; there was a real necessity; he acted in good faith; and he acted as a prudent person would in his own case.
concepts.analogy: Authority to build a house includes authority to buy the bricks; and if a flood hits the site, the site manager may move the cement to safety without phoning the owner.
concepts.work: Transporters and clearing agents often face emergencies — spoiling perishables, port delays. A CA checks whether expenses claimed under emergency authority meet the Section 189 test.

concepts.title: Sub-agents and substituted agents (Sections 190–195)
body: Section 190: an agent cannot ordinarily delegate — the principal chose him personally. Delegation is allowed where the custom of trade permits it or the nature of the agency requires it.

Sub-agent (Section 191): someone engaged by the original agent who works under that agent's directions. If properly appointed (Section 192), the principal is bound by his acts as if he were an original agent; the agent is responsible to the principal for the sub-agent's acts; the sub-agent is responsible to the agent, and to the principal only for fraud or wilful wrong. If improperly appointed (Section 193), the principal is not bound; the agent is responsible for the sub-agent's acts to both principal and third persons.

Substituted agent (Sections 194–195): a person whom the agent, having express or implied authority, names to act for the principal. He is the principal's own agent for that part of the business; privity of contract exists between him and the principal. The original agent is not responsible for him, provided he used the discretion of a man of ordinary prudence in selecting him.
concepts.analogy: A sub-agent is the agent's assistant; a substituted agent is a new agent introduced to the principal and then left to report to him directly.
concepts.work: A CA firm engaged for an audit cannot outsource the engagement to another firm without the client's consent; where component auditors are appointed, engagement letters spell out whether they act under the principal auditor or report directly to the client.

concepts.title: Duties of an agent (Sections 211–218)
body: Follow instructions or, absent instructions, the custom of the business — and make good any loss from not doing so (Section 211). Act with reasonable skill and diligence and compensate for direct consequences of negligence or misconduct (Section 212). Render proper accounts on demand (Section 213). In difficulty, use reasonable diligence to communicate with the principal and seek instructions (Section 214).

Not deal on his own account without the principal's consent: if he does so without disclosing all material facts, the principal may repudiate the transaction (Section 215) or claim from the agent any benefit he made (Section 216).

Not make secret profits; not delegate (Section 190); pay to the principal all sums received on his account, after the deductions he is entitled to (Section 218); and not misuse confidential information gained in the agency.
concepts.analogy: An agent is a trusted steward: obey, be careful, keep accounts, ask when unsure, never feather your own nest, and hand over what belongs to the master.
concepts.work: Commission agents, C&F agents and stockbrokers all owe these duties. Forensic accountants often trace undisclosed "own-account" deals by agents and quantify the profit recoverable under Section 216.

concepts.title: Rights of an agent (Sections 217–225)
body: Retainer (Section 217): from money received for the principal, the agent may keep what is due to him for advances, expenses properly incurred and remuneration.

Remuneration (Section 219): payable only when the act is completed, unless otherwise agreed; an agent guilty of misconduct in the business is not entitled to remuneration for that part of the business (Section 220).

Lien (Section 221): unless otherwise agreed, the agent may retain the principal's goods, papers and other property received by him until his commission, disbursements and services are paid or accounted for. The lien is lost if possession is lost, or waived.

Indemnity: for the consequences of all lawful acts done in exercise of his authority (Section 222); for acts done in good faith that cause injury to third persons (Section 223) — but not for criminal acts (Section 224); and compensation for injury caused by the principal's neglect or want of skill (Section 225).

concepts.analogy: The agent is allowed to take his fee and costs out of the money he collects — like a waiter keeping the agreed tip from the bill he collects for the restaurant.
concepts.work: In consignment accounting, the account sales prepared by the agent shows exactly these deductions — commission, expenses — before remitting the balance. CAs reconcile account sales with the consignor's books.

concepts.title: Principal's liability to third parties (Sections 226–229, 237–238)
body: Section 226: contracts made and acts done by an agent within his authority bind the principal as if done by him personally.

Agent exceeding authority: if the authorised part can be separated from the unauthorised part, the principal is bound only by the authorised part (Section 227); if it cannot be separated, the principal need not recognise the transaction (Section 228). But where the principal has led third persons to believe the acts were within authority, he is bound (Section 237).

Notice to the agent, given in the course of the business, is notice to the principal (Section 229). The principal is liable for fraud, misrepresentation or wrongs committed by the agent in the course of his business, as if he had done them himself (Section 238).
concepts.analogy: The principal answers for his agent's work like an owner answers for his shop counter — even for mistakes made behind it during business hours.
concepts.work: Misselling by a company's sales agents creates liability for the company. Auditors assess such claims for provisions and contingent-liability disclosure.

concepts.title: Personal liability of the agent (Sections 230–235)
body: Section 230: unless otherwise agreed, an agent cannot personally enforce contracts made for his principal, nor is he personally bound by them. The agent is presumed to be personally liable where: (1) he buys or sells goods for a merchant who lives outside India; (2) he does not disclose the name of the principal; (3) the principal, though disclosed, cannot be sued (e.g. a minor) — unless the third party knew; (4) he is a pretended agent and the principal disowns the act (Section 235); (5) he exceeds his authority, misleading the third party (breach of warranty of authority).

Undisclosed principal (Section 231): if the other party did not know he was dealing with an agent, the principal may enforce the contract but takes it subject to the defences available against the agent; if the principal reveals himself before completion, the other party may refuse to go on if he can show he would not have contracted with him. Section 233: where the agent is personally liable, the third party may hold either the agent or the principal, or both, liable. Section 234: if the third party, knowing the facts, makes the agent alone (or the principal alone) liable, he cannot later turn to the other.
concepts.analogy: Normally the agent is only a messenger; but if he hides the sender, pretends to be a messenger, or sends a parcel for a sender who cannot be traced, he must answer himself.
concepts.work: Import agents often sign purchase contracts for foreign principals. A CA advising such an agent warns that, under Section 230, he may be personally liable unless the contract clearly excludes it.

concepts.title: Termination of agency (Sections 201–210)
body: Modes (Section 201): revocation by the principal; renunciation by the agent; completion of the business; death or unsoundness of mind of either party; insolvency of the principal; expiry of the agreed term. (Dissolution of a firm or winding up of a company that is principal has the same effect.)

Irrevocable agency (Section 202): if the agent has his own stake in the very property the agency deals with, the agency cannot (unless the contract expressly says so) be brought to an end so as to harm that stake — not even by the principal's death or insanity. Example: authority to sell land and repay oneself a debt from the proceeds.

The principal may revoke at any time until the agent has used the authority in a way that binds the principal (Section 203), but not as regards acts and obligations already arising from acts done (Section 204). Premature revocation or renunciation of a fixed-term agency without sufficient cause requires compensation (Section 205); reasonable notice must be given (Section 206). Revocation may be express or implied (Section 207).

Effect (Section 208): termination takes effect against the agent when it becomes known to him, and against third persons when it becomes known to them. On the principal's death or insanity, the agent must still take reasonable steps to protect the principal's interests (Section 209). Termination of the agent's authority ends a sub-agent's authority too (Section 210).
concepts.analogy: Ending an agency is like switching off a light that others are still seeing by: it goes dark for the agent when he is told, and for outsiders when they are told.
concepts.work: When a company removes an authorised signatory, the CA advises it to inform banks and major suppliers at once — until they are told, Section 208 may still bind the company to the old signatory's acts.

illustrations.title: A minor as agent
illustrations.q: Ojas appoints Pihu, aged 16, to sell his motorbike for not less than ₹90,000. Pihu sells it to Rahul for ₹75,000. (a) Is Ojas bound by the sale? (b) Can Ojas recover the ₹15,000 shortfall from Pihu?

solution.provision: Section 184: as between the principal and third persons, any person may become an agent, but a minor agent is not responsible to the principal. Section 183: the principal must be a major of sound mind — here he is.
solution.facts: Ojas (major) appointed Pihu (minor). She sold for ₹75,000 against an instruction of a minimum of ₹90,000.
solution.analysis: The sale was made by an agent within the kind of act she was appointed to do, so Ojas is bound as against Rahul. Because Pihu is a minor, she cannot be held responsible to Ojas for disobeying instructions.
solution.conclusion: (a) Ojas is bound by the sale to Rahul. (b) Ojas cannot recover the ₹15,000 shortfall from Pihu.

illustrations.title: Perishables in a strike — emergency authority
illustrations.q: Sumit, a transporter, is carrying 8 tonnes of grapes from Nashik to Delhi for Tanvi. A sudden transport strike blocks the highway for several days. Sumit tries to call Tanvi, but she is on a flight abroad and unreachable. The grapes start rotting, so Sumit sells them in the nearest market at the best price available. Tanvi sues Sumit for selling without authority. Decide.

solution.provision: Section 189: when an emergency arises, an agent may do whatever is needed to shield the principal from loss that a person of ordinary prudence would do in his own case under similar circumstances. The agent should be unable to communicate with the principal, there must be real necessity, and he must act in good faith.
solution.facts: The grapes were perishable and began rotting because of an unforeseen strike. Sumit tried but failed to reach Tanvi, and sold at the best available price.
solution.analysis: All conditions are met: genuine emergency, perishable goods, failed attempt to communicate, and a sale that a prudent owner would make to cut losses. Sumit acted as an agent of necessity.
solution.conclusion: Sumit is not liable. Tanvi is bound by the sale and is entitled to the sale proceeds (less proper expenses).

illustrations.title: Agent's account: what can he retain?
illustrations.q: Prakash appoints Qamar as his selling agent at a commission of 5% on sales. Qamar sells 320 cartons of detergent at ₹1,500 each and receives the money. He paid ₹7,200 freight and ₹4,800 godown rent on Prakash's behalf. Prepare the account Qamar should render and state the amount payable to Prakash.

solution.provision: Section 213: the agent must render proper accounts. Section 217: he may retain, out of sums received for the principal, all moneys due to him for advances, expenses properly incurred and remuneration. Section 218: he must pay the balance to the principal. Section 219: remuneration is due on completion of the act.
solution.analysis: Qamar may deduct his commission and the expenses properly incurred for Prakash before remitting. ₹4,80,000 − ₹24,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹4,44,000.
solution.conclusion: Qamar must pay ₹4,44,000 to Prakash, with the account below.

illustrations.title: Agent buys the principal's property himself
illustrations.q: Usha engages Vinod to sell her flat. Vinod tells her the best offer is ₹9,50,000 and, without disclosing that the "buyer" is his own brother-in-law acting for him, gets her to agree. Two months later Vinod resells the flat for ₹11,50,000. What are Usha's rights?

solution.provision: Section 215: if an agent deals on his own account without the principal's consent and without disclosing all material facts, the principal may repudiate the transaction if the agent dishonestly concealed facts or the dealing was disadvantageous to him. Section 216: if an agent, without the principal's knowledge, deals on his own account, the principal may claim from him any benefit resulting from the transaction.
solution.facts: Vinod bought the flat for himself through a relative at ₹9,50,000, concealing this, and resold it for ₹11,50,000 — a gain of ₹2,00,000.
solution.analysis: Vinod dealt on his own account without disclosure. Since the flat has been resold to a third party, repudiation is no longer practical; but Usha can recover the benefit Vinod made.
solution.conclusion: Usha can claim ₹2,00,000 from Vinod under Section 216 (she could have repudiated the sale under Section 215 had the flat not been resold). Vinod also forfeits any commission for this misconduct (Section 220).

checks.label: profit made by the agent on resale

jobs.title: Removing an authorised signatory
jobs.situation: Your company's purchase manager has resigned. He was authorised to place orders up to ₹10 lakh with approved vendors.
steps: Pass an internal approval revoking his authority from the date of leaving.
Write to all approved vendors and banks informing them — under Section 208 termination is effective against third parties only when they come to know of it.
Collect his purchase order book, digital signature tokens and system access.
Review orders placed in his last week and confirm them or cancel promptly.
jobs.takeaway: Authority ends inside the company on a date; outside the company it ends only when third parties are told.
jobs.think: If a vendor who was never informed accepts an order from him a week after he leaves, is the company bound?
jobs.answer: Very likely yes — the vendor did not know of the termination (Section 208), and the company had held him out as its agent (Section 237).

jobs.title: Commission agent's account sales
jobs.situation: The client's agent in Kolkata remitted ₹38 lakh against sales of ₹42 lakh, deducting commission ₹2.1 lakh and "miscellaneous expenses" ₹1.9 lakh.
steps: Check the commission rate in the agency agreement (5% of ₹42 lakh = ₹2.1 lakh — agrees).
Ask for supporting bills for the miscellaneous expenses: only expenses properly incurred for the principal can be retained (Section 217).
Disallow and recover any unsupported amount; it is a sum received on the principal's account that must be paid over (Section 218).
Recommend periodic accounts from the agent (Section 213).
jobs.takeaway: An agent may deduct only what the law and the contract allow — everything else belongs to the principal.
jobs.think: If ₹60,000 of the expenses is unsupported, how much more should the agent remit?

jobs.title: Agent for a foreign supplier
jobs.role: CA advising an Indian trading company
jobs.situation: Your client signs contracts with Indian buyers for the sale of machines manufactured by a German company, signing "for and on behalf of" the German principal.
steps: Explain Section 230: an agent selling goods for a merchant resident abroad is presumed to be personally liable unless the contract shows otherwise.
Recommend an express clause in each buyer contract excluding the agent's personal liability.
Ensure the agency agreement with the German company gives the client an indemnity (Section 222) for claims arising from authorised acts.
Disclose any guarantees or performance obligations in the client's financial statements.
jobs.takeaway: With foreign principals, the agent is presumed to be on the hook — draft around it.
jobs.think: Would the presumption apply if the principal were a company in Mumbai?
jobs.answer: No. For a disclosed principal resident in India, the general rule applies — the agent is not personally liable unless he agreed to be.

mcqs.q: Under Section 182, someone engaged to act for another person, or to stand in for him when dealing with outsiders, is called:
mcqs.explain: Section 182: an agent is someone engaged to act for another person or to stand in for him when dealing with outsiders; the person he acts for is the principal. The tempting trap is "a bailee" — a bailee holds goods for a purpose but does not represent the owner in dealings with others. A partner is an agent of the firm, but agency is far wider than partnership. In practice: a clearing and forwarding agent handling customs for an importer acts as the importer's agent.

mcqs.q: Who may employ an agent under Section 183?
mcqs.explain: Section 183: only a person who is a major under his personal law and of sound mind can appoint an agent. The principal must be competent to contract, because the agent's acts become his. The tempting trap is "any person including a minor" — a minor cannot appoint an agent, since he cannot contract himself. In practice: a power of attorney signed by a minor is invalid; a guardian must act instead.

mcqs.q: A minor appointed as an agent:
options: Can bind the principal to third parties but is not liable to the principal
Cannot act as an agent at all
Is personally liable to the principal for negligence
mcqs.explain: Section 184: as between principal and third persons, any person, even a minor, may become an agent, so the minor's acts bind the principal. But a person who is not of majority and sound mind is not responsible to the principal. The tempting trap is "cannot act as an agent at all" — agency capacity depends on the principal, not the agent. In practice: a business that uses a 17-year-old to collect payments is bound by his receipts but cannot sue him for negligence under the agency.

mcqs.q: Consideration for creating an agency is:
mcqs.explain: Section 185: an agency can be created without any consideration. A friend who agrees to act for you without payment is still your agent, with the same authority and duties. The tempting trap is "essential", carried over from the general rule that agreements without consideration are void. In practice: family members often act as unpaid agents under a power of attorney to manage bank accounts or property for relatives living abroad.

mcqs.q: Which of the following CANNOT be ratified?
options: An act that is void, such as a forged signature
A purchase made on the principal's behalf without authority
A loan of the principal's money made without authority
A sale made on the principal's behalf without authority
mcqs.explain: Ratification (Sections 196 to 200) can validate only acts that the principal could lawfully have authorised. A void act, such as forging the principal's signature, cannot be ratified, and nor can an illegal act. The tempting trap is the unauthorised loan of the principal's money — though unauthorised, it is a lawful act and can be ratified. Ratification also cannot injure third parties. In practice: a company cannot adopt a forged cheque, but its board can approve a purchase a manager made without authority.

mcqs.q: The principal accepts the beneficial part of an unauthorised transaction but rejects the rest. Under Section 199:
options: He is taken to have ratified the whole transaction
He has ratified only the beneficial part
There is no ratification at all
mcqs.explain: Section 199: a person ratifying any unauthorised act done on his behalf ratifies the whole transaction of which that act formed part. He cannot accept the benefits and reject the burdens. The tempting trap is "he has ratified only the beneficial part" — the law does not allow selective ratification. In practice: a company that accepts goods bought by an unauthorised manager must also honour the payment terms of that purchase.

mcqs.q: In an emergency, an agent may act to protect his principal from loss as:
options: A person of ordinary prudence would in his own case (Section 189)
mcqs.explain: Section 189: in an emergency, an agent has authority to do all acts to protect his principal from loss as a person of ordinary prudence would do in his own case under similar circumstances. The tempting trap is "the principal expressly instructed" — in an emergency, the agent may not be able to contact the principal, and the law gives him extended authority. In practice: a transporter carrying perishable goods may sell them en route if they are about to rot and the owner cannot be reached.

mcqs.q: A person engaged by the original agent and working under that agent's directions is called:
mcqs.explain: Section 191: a sub-agent is someone the original agent engages, and who works under that agent's direction, in the business of the agency. The tempting trap is "a substituted agent" — that person is named by the agent at the principal's express or implied authority to act for the principal directly, not under the agent's control. In practice: when a CA firm engaged by a client outsources part of the work to another firm under its own supervision, that firm acts as a sub-agent.

mcqs.q: Privity of contract exists between the principal and:
options: No one except the original agent
mcqs.explain: A substituted agent, named by the agent with the principal's authority, becomes the principal's own agent (Section 194), so there is privity of contract between them. A sub-agent, even if properly appointed, is responsible to the agent, not the principal, except for fraud or wilful wrong. The tempting trap is "a properly appointed sub-agent" — proper appointment binds the principal to third parties but creates no privity. In practice: a property owner who authorises his broker to appoint a local broker directly can deal with that local broker himself.
mcqs.topic: Difference between a Sub-agent and a Substituted Agent

mcqs.q: An agent sells to himself the principal's goods without disclosure, and the deal is disadvantageous to the principal. The principal may:
options: Repudiate the transaction or claim the agent's benefit
Do nothing as the goods are sold
mcqs.explain: Section 215: if an agent deals on his own account without the principal's consent, and either conceals material facts dishonestly or the dealing is disadvantageous, the principal may repudiate the transaction. Section 216 lets the principal claim any benefit the agent made. The tempting trap is "only claim the agreed commission" — the principal has far stronger remedies. In practice: a broker who quietly buys his client's property at a low price can be forced to undo the deal or hand over the profit.
mcqs.topic: Duties and Obligations of an Agent

mcqs.q: An agent sells goods for ₹6,00,000 at 3% commission and has paid ₹9,000 expenses for the principal. How much must he pay over?
mcqs.explain: Commission = 3% × ₹6,00,000 = ₹18,000. Under Sections 217 and 218 the agent may deduct his commission and expenses properly incurred before paying over: ₹6,00,000 − ₹18,000 − ₹9,000 = ₹5,73,000. The tempting trap is ₹5,82,000, deducting only commission. In practice: a selling agent sends the principal an account sales showing gross sales, commission and expenses, with the net amount remitted.

mcqs.q: An agent is NOT entitled to indemnity from the principal for:
options: A criminal act done at the principal's request
Lawful acts done in exercise of authority
Acts done in good faith that injure third persons
Expenses properly incurred in the agency
mcqs.explain: Section 224: a principal is not liable to indemnify an agent for a criminal act, even if the principal employed him to do it. Sections 222 and 223, by contrast, give indemnity for lawful acts in the exercise of authority and for acts done in good faith that injure third persons. The tempting trap is the good-faith option, which sounds risky but is protected. In practice: an employee told to falsify accounts cannot later claim reimbursement of fines from his employer.

mcqs.q: An agent is presumed to be personally liable when he contracts on behalf of:
options: A disclosed principal resident in India
mcqs.explain: Section 230: an agent generally cannot be sued on contracts made for his principal, but he is presumed personally liable where he buys or sells goods on behalf of a merchant living abroad, where he does not disclose his principal's name, or where the principal, though disclosed, cannot be sued. The tempting trap is "a company registered in India" — such a disclosed principal can be sued directly. In practice: Indian import agents of foreign suppliers are careful about their personal exposure.
mcqs.topic: Personal Liability of Agent to Third Parties

mcqs.q: Kavi owes Lal ₹3,00,000 and authorises Lal to sell Kavi's plot and recover the debt from the sale price. Kavi dies before the sale. The agency:
options: Is not terminated — agency coupled with interest (Section 202)
mcqs.explain: Section 202: when the agent has his own interest in the property he is dealing with, the agency cannot, unless agreed, be ended in a way that harms that interest — not even by the principal's death. Lal is to recover his ₹3,00,000 from the sale, so the agency survives Kavi's death. The tempting trap is "terminates on Kavi's death", the normal Section 201 rule. In practice: lenders take irrevocable powers of attorney to sell secured property for recovery of their dues.

mcqs.q: As regards third persons, termination of an agent's authority takes effect:
options: When it becomes known to them
From the date of the principal's decision
When the agent returns the papers
mcqs.explain: Section 208: termination of an agent's authority takes effect, as regards third persons, only when it becomes known to them. Until then, third parties can rely on the agent's apparent authority. The tempting trap is "from the date of the principal's decision" — that applies between principal and agent, but outsiders are protected until they learn of it. In practice: companies that remove an authorised signatory notify banks and major suppliers in writing at once.

mcqs.q: On which person's insolvency is an agency terminated under Section 201?
mcqs.explain: Section 201 lists the ways an agency ends: revocation by the principal, renunciation by the agent, completion of the business, death or unsoundness of mind of either principal or agent, and the principal being adjudicated insolvent. Only the principal's insolvency terminates the agency. The tempting trap is "the agent" — the agent's death or unsoundness of mind ends it, but not his insolvency. In practice: when a business is declared insolvent, the authority of its agents ends and the insolvency professional takes over.

questions.q: Wasim, without any authority, buys 50 sacks of sugar from Xavier "on behalf of Yusuf". Yusuf, on learning of it, sells 20 sacks to his own customers at a profit, but refuses to pay for the remaining 30, saying he never authorised the purchase. Is Yusuf liable for the price of all 50 sacks?

questions.q: Zara owes Arjun ₹4,00,000. She appoints Arjun as her agent to sell her shop and authorises him to repay himself the debt out of the sale proceeds. Before the sale, Zara writes to revoke Arjun's authority, and a week later she dies. Can Arjun go ahead with the sale?

model.provision: Section 202: if the agent has his own stake in the very property the agency deals with, the agency cannot — unless the contract expressly provides otherwise — be ended in a way that harms that stake.

model.analysis: Arjun's authority is coupled with an interest in the very property he is to sell. Neither Zara's revocation nor her death can end the agency to the prejudice of that interest.
model.conclusion: The agency is irrevocable. Arjun may sell the shop and recover ₹4,00,000 from the proceeds, accounting for any balance to Zara's estate.

questions.q: (a) State the cases in which an agent is personally liable to third parties. (3 marks) (b) Bina, the wife of Chetan, has for two years bought groceries on credit from Dev Stores, and Chetan has always paid the bills. Chetan then tells Bina to stop, but does not inform Dev Stores. Bina buys groceries worth ₹18,000 on credit. Is Chetan liable? (3 marks)

model.text: (a) Section 230: an agent normally cannot enforce, and is not bound by, contracts made for his principal. He is presumed to be personally liable where:

items: he buys or sells goods on behalf of a merchant living outside India;
he does not disclose the name of his principal;
the principal, though disclosed, cannot be sued (e.g. a minor or a non-existent company), unless the other party knew;
he is a pretended agent and the principal disowns the act (Section 235);
he exceeds his authority and is liable for breach of warranty of authority;
he has expressly agreed to be personally liable.

model.provision: Section 237 (agency by estoppel): where a principal, by his words or conduct, has induced third persons to believe that acts done by an agent are within his authority, he is bound by them. Under Section 208, termination of authority takes effect against third persons only when it becomes known to them.
model.facts: Chetan had for two years paid for groceries bought by Bina on credit from Dev Stores. He withdrew her authority but did not tell Dev Stores, who supplied ₹18,000 more.
model.analysis: By his past conduct Chetan held out Bina as his agent. Dev Stores was not told of the withdrawal and acted on that belief.
model.conclusion: Chetan is liable to pay Dev Stores ₹18,000.

cases.title: Eshan, the export agent
cases.case: Farida, a carpet maker in Bhadohi, appoints Eshan as her agent to sell carpets in Delhi at a commission of 2% on sales. Eshan sells carpets for ₹24,00,000 and spends ₹15,000 on transport, which Farida had agreed to bear. Without telling Farida, Eshan appoints his cousin Gopal to handle some sales; Gopal misappropriates ₹60,000 of the sale proceeds. Separately, Eshan signs a contract "as agent" with Henrik, a buyer in Norway, to sell him carpets made by Farida, without naming her.

mcqs.q: How much commission is Eshan entitled to?
mcqs.explain: Section 219 entitles the agent to the agreed remuneration once the act is completed. Commission = 2% × ₹24,00,000 = ₹48,000. The tempting trap is ₹63,000, which wrongly adds the ₹15,000 transport expense to the commission — expenses are reimbursed separately. In practice: agents' commissions are recorded as selling expenses by the principal, and TDS under the Income-tax Act may apply when commission crosses the threshold.

mcqs.q: Before accounting for Gopal's misappropriation, how much must Eshan pay over to Farida?
mcqs.explain: Sections 217 and 218 let the agent retain his commission and expenses properly incurred before paying over the sale proceeds: ₹24,00,000 − ₹48,000 − ₹15,000 = ₹23,37,000. The tempting trap is ₹23,52,000, deducting commission only and forgetting the agreed transport cost. In practice: the principal's accountant reconciles the agent's account sales against goods dispatched and the remittance received.

mcqs.q: Who bears the ₹60,000 misappropriated by Gopal, as between Farida and Eshan?
options: Eshan — Gopal was an improperly appointed sub-agent (Section 193)
Nobody — it is a loss of the third party
mcqs.explain: Eshan appointed Gopal without Farida's knowledge or authority, so Gopal is an improperly appointed sub-agent. Section 193 makes the agent responsible for such a sub-agent's acts both to the principal and to third persons. So Eshan bears the ₹60,000 as between him and Farida. The tempting trap is "Farida — she is the principal"; she never authorised the delegation. In practice: agency agreements usually forbid sub-delegation without written consent for exactly this reason.

mcqs.q: Can Henrik hold Eshan personally liable on the Norway contract?
options: Yes — the principal was not named (Section 230)
No — an agent is never personally liable
Only if Henrik is resident in India
mcqs.explain: Section 230 presumes an agent personally liable where he does not disclose the name of his principal. Eshan signed "as agent" but did not name Farida, so Henrik can hold Eshan personally liable. The tempting trap is "only if Henrik is resident in India" — the "merchant resident abroad" rule concerns where the principal lives, and is not what applies here. In practice: export agents usually name the manufacturer in the contract to avoid personal liability for its performance.
